title: Pandas Plotting Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on plotting with pandas and matplotlib: DataFrame.plot chart kinds, the figure and axes model, grouped plots, seaborn basics, and labelling and saving figures.

chapters.title: Plotting Mental Model
points: df.plot() and s.plot() are thin wrappers over matplotlib and return an Axes object; the index becomes the x-axis and each numeric column becomes one series
Figure = whole canvas, Axes = one plot area with its own x/y axis; plt.subplots() returns (fig, ax) and is preferred over the implicit plt state machine
Pyplot (plt.plot, plt.title) acts on the 'current' axes implicitly; the object API (ax.plot, ax.set_title) acts on an explicit axes and scales to multiple plots
Pandas vs seaborn vs raw matplotlib: pandas is fastest for quick wide-form plots, seaborn gives statistical plots from long-form data, matplotlib gives full control
Gotcha: plot() ignores non-numeric columns silently, and in scripts nothing shows until plt.show() is called (notebooks render automatically)

chapters.title: DataFrame.plot Chart Kinds
points: kind= selects the chart: 'line' (default), 'bar', 'barh', 'hist', 'box', 'scatter', 'area', 'pie'; df.plot.bar() is the equivalent accessor form
Line: df.plot(x='date', y='sales') or set the index to the date column; best for ordered or time-series data, one line per column
Bar: df['city'].value_counts().plot.bar() or df.plot.bar(x='city', y='sales'); stacked=True stacks columns, barh flips to horizontal for long labels
Hist: df['age'].plot.hist(bins=20) shows a distribution of one numeric variable; bins controls resolution, alpha=0.5 helps overlay several columns
Scatter: df.plot.scatter(x='height', y='weight', c='age', s=20) needs both x and y named; c colors and s sizes the points to show a third variable

chapters.title: Figure and Axes Control
points: fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 6)) creates a grid; axes is a 2D NumPy array, so index it as axes[0, 1] (flatten with axes.ravel())
Pass ax=axes[0] to df.plot(...) to draw into a chosen subplot; without ax= pandas makes a new figure or reuses the current axes
subplots=True on df.plot gives one subplot per column; sharex=True and sharey=True align the scales; layout=(2, 2) sets the grid
Two scales: df['a'].plot(ax=ax) then df['b'].plot(ax=ax, secondary_y=True), or ax2 = ax.twinx() in matplotlib
fig.tight_layout() prevents overlapping labels, while ax.set_xlim and ax.set_ylim, ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45) and ax.legend(loc='upper left') adjust limits, ticks and legend

chapters.title: Plotting Grouped Data
points: Aggregate before plotting: df.groupby('city')['sales'].sum().plot.bar() gives one bar per group; groupby returns an index of group keys that becomes the x-axis
Several metrics per group: df.groupby('city')[['sales','profit']].mean().plot.bar() draws grouped (side-by-side) bars, add stacked=True to stack them
Two keys: df.groupby(['year','city'])['sales'].sum().unstack().plot() pivots the inner key into columns, giving one series per city
df.pivot_table(index='month', columns='region', values='sales', aggfunc='sum').plot() is the readable alternative to groupby plus unstack

df.groupby('city')['sales'].plot(legend=True) draws one line per group on a shared axes, while df.plot.hist(by='city') or df.boxplot(by='city') splits into subplots, so check the result before assuming overlay

chapters.title: Seaborn Basics
points: import seaborn as sns; sns.set_theme() applies a cleaner default style; seaborn draws on matplotlib axes, so ax.set_title and plt.savefig still work
Seaborn prefers long-form (tidy) data with data=df and column names as strings: sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='height', y='weight', hue='sex')
hue splits by color, style by marker, size by point size; this replaces the manual groupby loop for categorical splits
Common functions: histplot (kde=True), boxplot, barplot (mean with confidence interval by default), countplot (counts), heatmap (df.corr(), annot=True), pairplot

Axes-level functions (scatterplot, histplot) take ax= and return an Axes, while figure-level ones (relplot, catplot, displot, pairplot) create their own figure and return a FacetGrid; use col= or row= to facet

chapters.title: Labelling, Saving and Cheat Sheet
points: Label with ax.set_title('Sales'), ax.set_xlabel('Month'), ax.set_ylabel('Revenue'), or pass title= to df.plot; always add units and a legend when there are multiple series
Save with fig.savefig('out.png', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight'); call savefig BEFORE plt.show(), because show() clears the figure and leaves a blank file
Output format follows the file extension (.png, .svg, .pdf); use transparent=True for a see-through background, and plt.close(fig) in loops to avoid memory leaks

Cheat sheet: df.plot(kind=, x=, y=, title=, figsize=, ax=, legend=, grid=, color=) | plt.subplots(r, c) | groupby().agg().plot.bar() | sns.<fn>(data=, x=, y=, hue=) | savefig(dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
Common mistakes: forgetting plt.show() in scripts, plotting unaggregated rows as bars, mixing the pyplot and object APIs on the wrong axes, and calling savefig after show
